bullets.title: US-Iran war escalates with Hormuz closure threat; oil spikes, shipping disrupted
bullets.body: The US launched its third round of strikes on Iran within a week targeting missile systems, air defenses, and IRGC boats near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran declared the Strait 'closed until further notice,' attacked US military sites in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan, and struck commercial vessels including a Qatari LNG tanker. Despite Iran's rhetoric, CENTCOM confirmed 140+ ships transited the strait in the past week and Trump stated Hormuz remained open to commercial shipping; CNN/UBS data showed Hormuz traffic declining noticeably. Market consensus held that a full closure was unlikely but JP Morgan warned oil was reassuming its role as market driver, with Brent spiking ~8% intraweek before partially retracing. Prediction markets put Hormuz normalization by July 31 at only 5% (down 22pp)—a material risk-premium event for energy prices and inflationary readings.

bullets.title: Fed hawkishness re-emerges: June FOMC minutes show inflation-centric shift; Warsh task forces signal regime change
bullets.body: June FOMC minutes showed the most hawkish rhetoric since 2022, with 'almost all' participants willing to tighten if inflation remains elevated and Fed staff revising core PCE arrival at 2% out to end-2028. Governor Waller stated inflation risks have 'completely flipped' from labor-market concerns, and prediction markets priced ~37% probability of a September hike (up 10pp on the week). Separately, new Fed Chair Warsh unveiled five expert task forces covering communications, balance sheet, data, AI/productivity, and inflation frameworks—including Marc Andreessen and former AZ governor Taylor White—signaling potential overhaul of dot-plot guidance and exploration of a higher neutral rate. Analysts at 22V and Wolfe flagged that benign next-week CPI/PPI (~0.21% MoM PCE) would support a higher-neutral-rate/risk-on thesis, while a hot print (>0.3%) would push yields higher and pressure cyclicals.

bullets.title: META Muse Spark 1.1 catalyzes AI infrastructure re-rating; $250B 2027 capex implies demand broadening
bullets.body: Meta's release of Muse Spark 1.1—a frontier-class agentic/coding model priced 25% below Anthropic/OpenAI alternatives—and announcement of plans to double compute capacity to 14GW by 2027 (~$250B capex vs. prior $175-225B estimates) triggered a sector-wide re-rating. META stock rose ~11% over two days (largest gain since April 2025) as SemiAnalysis published a positive take on META's AI infrastructure monetization, and multiple sell-side analysts raised price targets (KeyBanc to $790, Mizuho upgraded). The capex news was read as bullish confirmation that AI infrastructure demand is broadening beyond hyperscalers, reversing the narrative that Meta was scaling back. META also announced a custom Iris AI chip entering production in September via AVGO partnership with TSMC manufacturing.

bullets.title: AI capex debt bubble concern surfaces alongside record hyperscaler bond issuance
bullets.body: Amazon priced a $25B eight-tranche bond sale—its fourth debt raise YTD totaling ~$53B—in the same week that total hyperscaler IG bond issuance YTD exceeded all of 2023. JPMorgan credit downgraded MSFT and META on heavy capex funding risks and unclear AI ROIC, while upgrading ORCL as best-positioned hyperscaler on credit metrics. Jefferies, 22V, and other strategists flagged that cumulative AI debt could reach $7T by 2029, making it the second-largest asset-backed debt market, but noted that 4% aggregate corporate debt growth vs. 12% during the TMT boom suggests systemic risk is contained—for now. Goldman's asset management team flagged data center construction growth slowing materially, a potential leading indicator of capex moderation.

bullets.title: Memory supercycle accelerating: SK Hynix prices $26.5B record US ADR offering; CEO warns shortage extends past 2030
bullets.body: SK Hynix priced its US ADR listing (temp ticker SKHYV) at $149—the largest-ever US equity offering by a foreign company, 7x+ oversubscribed—and opened at $170 (+14%). The SK Hynix CEO warned at the listing that 2027 will be the worst year in memory industry history from a supply perspective and that demand will outpace supply into the next decade. SIA May data showed memory sales at record $74.6B (+32% MoM); Taiwan DRAM exports up 158% in H1 2026. Micron announced $250B in US fab investment through 2035 (raised from $200B) and poured the first concrete for its New York megafab, signing a strategic customer agreement with Ford. Analyst consensus sees DRAM contracts up 20-30% QoQ in 3Q and HBM4E bit-exchange premiums of 4-5x DRAM as structurally underappreciated.

bullets.title: NVDA Rubin (Kyber rack) delayed to 2028 on PCB constraints; China H200 approvals offer partial offset
bullets.body: SemiAnalysis reported NVIDIA's Kyber NVL144 rack delayed 12+ months to 2028 due to PCB midplane manufacturability issues, canceling the NVL72x2 architecture. NVIDIA denied delays, and an expert call cited by Midnight Capital confirmed the roadmap was intact. China separately was reported to be permitting limited H200 purchases (<200K units, training-only) for top AI firms including Alibaba and ByteDance, lifting NVDA ~4% on the news. NVIDIA also announced partnering with d-Matrix and plans to incorporate external chip architectures into its platform. Despite near-term sentiment volatility, JPMorgan and Citi maintained bullish views: JPMorgan noted 2027 Rubin estimates raised +7% and described NVDA at 10-year valuation lows vs. SPX as an opportunity, while Citi reaffirmed $300 PT.

bullets.title: Semiconductor momentum factor hit worst week since 2022; SOX down 11% before rebounding
bullets.body: The SOX experienced a 11% two-week drawdown—the seventh-largest in a decade—reached in 14 days, driven by Samsung Q2 earnings that missed elevated buy-side expectations despite record absolute profit, combined with crowded positioning unwind in leveraged Korean retail ETFs (KOSPI VIX hit 97). JPMorgan, Goldman, and Morgan Stanley characterized the selloff as technical/positioning-driven rather than fundamental, noting AI demand data (DRAM/NAND contracts, Taiwan chip exports, hyperscaler capex) remained robust. By week-end the sector staged a sharp recovery on AVGO-Apple deal news and META capex confirmation. Goldman noted the Mag7 trading at 10-year lows vs. SPX offered an entry point; JPMorgan's tactical bull view was maintained.

bullets.title: TSMC CoWoS packaging capacity raised again; AI packaging demand-supply gap now 20%
bullets.body: JPMorgan raised TSMC's CoWoS capacity estimates for the fourth time in 2026—to 115k/190k/225k wafer-starts-per-month for end-2026/27/28—driven by strong NVDA and AWS CPU demand. TSMC is accelerating AP7 Phase 2 capacity allocation to 50-60% CoWoS and expanding CoWoS-R. The agentic AI-driven CPU surge has widened the advanced-packaging demand-supply gap to ~20%. TSMC's 2Q earnings (July 16) are seen as the next critical catalyst: if management confirms AI demand visibility and capacity constraint, the sector could rebound sharply. Jefferies expects TSMC to guide 3Q revenue +10-12% QoQ vs. HSD consensus and potentially raise full-year guidance to 30-35% YoY growth.

bullets.title: Apple-Broadcom $30B+ deal through 2031 expands custom AI silicon scope; AAPL loses EU gatekeeper appeal
bullets.body: Apple and Broadcom announced a multiyear partnership exceeding $30B through 2031 for custom silicon and wireless connectivity, including development of new AI/datacenter ASICs and expansion of Broadcom's Fort Collins facility to produce 15B+ US-made chips. Analysts viewed the deal as securing Broadcom's RF and ASIC position against rivals and limiting QRVO/SWKS recapture potential. Separately, Apple filed a federal lawsuit against OpenAI alleging misappropriation of hardware trade secrets by former employees; OpenAI has hired ~400 people from Apple. The EU General Court upheld Apple's gatekeeper designation under the Digital Markets Act, requiring third-party App Store access compliance under threat of 10% global revenue fines.

bullets.title: Earnings season opens with elevated expectations; Q2 estimates revised up 3.4% in-quarter—best since 2021
bullets.body: With Q2 2026 earnings season beginning (Delta reported first; banks report July 14-15), Wall Street consensus is for ~20%+ EPS growth for the second consecutive quarter. Sell-side surveys and JPMorgan data show Q2 earnings estimates were revised up 3.4% during the quarter vs. a typical -2.0% five-year average—the largest upgrade since Q2 2021—with 11 of 11 S&P sectors showing revenue growth. Multiple strategists flagged the high bar: options markets are pricing ±5.1% earnings-day moves (above historical ±5.4% realized) with bullish tech/semi positioning at extremes. NFLX (Jul 16), ASML (Jul 15), and TSM (Jul 16) are cited as the most important prints for AI narrative direction.

bullets.title: China AI competition intensifying: DeepSeek developing own chip; US firms routing 30%+ of tokens to Chinese models
bullets.body: Reuters reported DeepSeek is developing proprietary AI inference chips to reduce reliance on NVIDIA and Huawei—compressing NVDA stock ~1.5%. Separately, MS TMT noted that Chinese open-source models (DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM) now represent >30% of US enterprise token usage vs. 11% a year ago, and Chinese firms plan to shift 46% of AI accelerator budgets to domestic chips. China also reportedly is considering restricting overseas access to its most advanced homegrown AI models, which could paradoxically benefit NVIDIA (Nemotron) and Google if enacted. Anthropic warned US lawmakers that Chinese AI models are catching up via distillation.

bullets.title: Quantum computing trade narrative shifted to execution-phase: June executive orders set 2028 deadlines
bullets.body: One twitter analyst noted that the June 22 executive orders transformed the quantum computing investment narrative from sentiment-driven to deadline-focused procurement, with a 2028 deadline for delivery of working quantum computers under the QC-ADDS mandate. Most market participants are still trading the old thesis. This is a sector-level signal rather than individual company catalysts, but directly relevant for QBTS and IONQ positioning.

bullets.title: 30-year Treasury hits 5.058%—highest since pre-GFC; bond market warning for equity multiples
bullets.body: The 30-year Treasury auction cleared at 5.058%, the highest level since the run-up to the Global Financial Crisis, and the 10-year yield climbed back above 4.55% intraweek. JPMorgan and 22V Research framed 4.5% 10Y as the equity warning level and 4.65-4.75% as a clear negative. Analysts noted S&P 500 Shiller P/E approaching Dot Com Bubble peak, the trailing-to-forward P/E gap at historically wide levels, and the VIX-single-stock IV divergence hitting record highs—all pointing to fragility. Wolfe and Hedgeye recommended buying MTUM hedges and XHB puts into earnings rather than broad index protection. Japan 10Y yields also hit 30-year highs (2.87%), reinforcing global rate normalization.

bullets.title: Meta AI capex monetization via cloud and developer API opens new revenue pathway
bullets.body: Beyond the infrastructure build, Meta announced paid access to Muse Spark 1.1 via developer APIs at $1.25/$4.25 per million input/output tokens—25% cheaper than Anthropic and OpenAI alternatives—and Zuckerberg confirmed plans to sell excess compute to external customers similar to AWS Bedrock. Brad Gerstner (Altimeter) on the All-In podcast predicted Anthropic could add $200B in revenue by 2027, with ARR already estimated at $47B-$69B depending on the source and accelerating at $550M/day. These dynamics suggest AI infrastructure providers (neocloud, power, memory) face durable demand from multiple customer tiers rather than just hyperscalers.

bullets.title: US margin debt nears Dot Com peak at 6.2% of M2; investor allocations to defensives at cycle lows
bullets.body: US margin debt as a share of M2 reached 6.2% in May—just below the 6.3% Dot Com peak. Simultaneously, AAII surveys showed stock allocations at 71% vs. a 61.5% historical average, and BofA data showed investor allocations to cash, bonds, and defensive stocks at cycle lows. High-Beta Momentum suffered its worst 5-day performance since COVID. These positioning signals suggest that a technical air pocket could develop heading into earnings season, particularly if AI capex narratives disappoint. UBS's proprietary market fragility index also hit an all-time high.

bullets.title: Japan pension pivot: Finance Minister pushes GPIF to increase domestic asset allocation; yen strengthens
bullets.body: Japan's Finance Minister Katayama announced measures to encourage GPIF and other pension funds to increase domestic asset investments, causing USD/JPY to drop 0.5-0.6% on the session and pushing JGB yields modestly lower. Japan June PPI came in at 7.1% YoY (above the 6.8% forecast), reinforcing the case for further BOJ tightening. MS and PSC flagged JPY shorts as crowded at a time when Japanese economic conditions are turning positive, with Takaichi administration reforms and asset manager repatriation themes gaining traction. The setup is emerging as a contrarian macro trade.

bullets.title: AI hiring paradox: companies using AI are growing headcount 10%; software job postings accelerating
bullets.body: Multiple sources confirmed AI adoption is net job-creating rather than destroying at the current stage. A Ramp study across 21,559 US firms showed companies adopting AI grew headcount ~10% over two years, with entry-level jobs growing 12%. Indeed's chief economist reported software development job postings growing faster than total job market. Sam Altman (OpenAI) confirmed AI has been 'net job-creating so far.' Separately, MS data showed 40% of AI adopters cited quantifiable benefits in Q2 2026 (vs. 21% a year prior), and enterprise AI spend is shifting from experimentation to deployment, consistent with AI theme names outperforming on earnings.
